nameStory: Buffalo-bur gets its name from its incredibly spiny, burr-like seed cases that stick to everything - just like the prairie where buffalo once roamed! The plant is so thoroughly armed with sharp spines that it earned colorful nicknames like 'bad woman' and 'Kansas thistle,' reflecting how unpleasant it is to encounter. When the plant dies, it breaks off and tumbles across the landscape like a prickly tumbleweed, spreading its seeds far and wide.
description: Buffalo-bur is a spiny annual plant that looks like it's wearing armor from head to toe. This prickly member of the nightshade family grows 3-5 feet tall and is covered in sharp spines on its stems, leaves, and even its flower buds. It produces cheerful yellow flowers that seem oddly welcoming on such a defensive plant, followed by berries enclosed in spiny cases that will definitely grab your attention (and your clothing).

idTips.label: Spines
idTips.description: Sharp, needle-like spines cover every part of the plant - stems, leaves, and flower buds feel like tiny daggers. These aren't soft prickles but genuine spines that can pierce through clothing and gloves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers are about 1 inch across with five pointed petals forming a star shape. The flowers have an unusual asymmetrical look with anthers of different sizes - some yellow, some darker.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed leaves look almost fern-like but feel rough and sandpapery to the touch. The leaves are divided into multiple segments with rounded lobes, and yes, they're covered in spines too.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small berries are completely enclosed in a spiny, inflated case that looks like a medieval weapon. These prickly pods dry out and easily attach to fur, clothing, or anything that brushes against them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a bushy, sprawling plant that becomes a tumbleweed when it dies. The whole plant has a grayish-green color and a rough, bristly texture that's unmistakable when you get close.

habitat: Buffalo-bur thrives in disturbed soils, roadsides, vacant lots, and agricultural areas throughout New England. It prefers sunny, dry locations with sandy or gravelly soil and is often found near railways, construction sites, or anywhere the ground has been disturbed. This western native has spread eastward and occasionally pops up in waste areas and along transportation corridors.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with the characteristic spiny, deeply-lobed leaves becoming visible in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom throughout the summer months, followed by the development of the distinctive spiny seed cases that make identification unmistakable.
seasonality.fall: Plants turn brown and brittle, often breaking free to tumble across the landscape as the spiny seed pods mature and release their contents.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems and persistent spiny seed cases may remain visible, but the annual plant has completed its life cycle.

funFact: Charles Darwin was so fascinated by buffalo-bur's unusual flower structure that he ordered seeds from America just over a week before he died, hoping to study why the flowers have two different sets of anthers - some for feeding bees and others for actual pollination!
confusionNotes: Despite its common name 'Kansas thistle,' buffalo-bur isn't a thistle at all but a nightshade related to tomatoes and potatoes. Real thistles have composite flowers made of many tiny florets, while buffalo-bur has single five-petaled flowers. Remember: true thistles have flower heads, buffalo-bur has star-shaped individual flowers.
contextualKnowledge: This plant has an interesting connection to garden pests - it's the original host of the Colorado potato beetle before that infamous bug discovered our potato crops in 1859 and became a major agricultural nightmare. The beetle found potatoes much more tasty than its spiny native host!
compareHints: Among New England nightshades, buffalo-bur is unmistakable due to its extreme spininess - no other Solanum species is nearly as heavily armed with spines. Carolina horsenettle has some prickles, but buffalo-bur looks like it's ready for medieval combat. The yellow flowers also set it apart from most other nightshades in our region, which typically have white or purple blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other nightshades in New England, bittersweet nightshade is the only one that grows as a climbing vine with purple flowers.
Among New England's nightshades, Carolina horsenettle is the only one covered in sharp prickles, making it instantly recognizable.
Unlike bittersweet nightshade which has purple flowers and grows as a climbing vine, eastern black nightshade has white flowers and grows as a low bushy annual.
Among its nightshade relatives in New England, tomato is easily distinguished by its large, edible red fruit and cultivation in gardens.
Black nightshade differs from its cousin bittersweet nightshade by being much smaller and having white flowers instead of purple ones with swept-back petals.
Unlike its nightshade relatives, potato has compound leaves rather than simple ones, and produces edible underground tubers.
Hairy nightshade differs from eastern black nightshade by its distinctly hairy stems and leaves (black nightshade is mostly smooth).

Green nightshade stands apart from its New England nightshade relatives primarily by its persistently green, glossy berries - eastern black nightshade and black nightshade both produce dark purple-black berries when ripe, while bittersweet nightshade produces bright red berries.
Unlike its wild nightshade relatives that grow as weeds in New England, cultivated eggplant is much larger in all aspects - bigger leaves, bigger flowers, and dramatically bigger fruits.

Garden huckleberry differs from other nightshades in New England by its drooping clusters of dark berries and relatively benign nature – unlike bittersweet nightshade with its bright red berries, or the more weedy black nightshade species.
Unlike other nightshades in New England, red buffalo-bur is the most heavily armed with prickles covering every surface.
